events.text: Cold. Cold everywhere, and grey, and heavy, and you at the bottom of it, one red point that will not go out. Above you the lid of the jar scrapes. A face comes down out of the dark, small, round, wrapped in a padded jacket, and a voice says, "No. No no no. Grandmother will kill me." The house has kept its fire alive for nine generations, and tonight the keeping was this child's, and the child fell asleep. Then the face sees you.

choices.text: Burn as bright as you can

effects.log: You swell, red and furious, a point of summer at the bottom of the jar. {npc} gasps, and blows, and feeds you a pine needle, and then another. By the time the cock crows the stove is lit and the rice is on, and {npc} is asleep on the kitchen floor beside the jar with one hand on its lid.

choices.text: Blink at the face

effects.log: You go dim and bright, dim and bright. {npc} stares. Then, very slowly, {he} blinks back. It is the first conversation of your life. {He} feeds you a pine needle as a reply, and you eat it, and it is delicious.

choices.text: Lie still in the ash and wait

effects.log: You stay small. {npc} digs, finds you, and breathes on you so softly that it is almost a question. You answer it by not going out. That is enough. By dawn there is a fire, and nobody else in the house ever knows how close it came.

events.text: Grandmother knows. Grandmothers always know. Grandmother stands over the fire jar in the grey morning, arms folded, and {npc} stands beside it with {his} head down, and nobody says anything for a long time. Then Grandmother speaks. "We do not tell the neighbours we nearly lost it. Not the Paks, not the Hans, not the priest. Nine generations. It did not go out." A long look into the jar, at you. "It did not go out." Quieter, this time.

choices.text: Flare up, so Grandmother can see you

effects.log: You burn up red under Grandmother's nose. The old woman steps back, and then forward again, and looks a long time. "Well. Somebody in there is stubborn." That night Grandmother banks the jar without help and talks to it the whole time, as if to a guest.

choices.text: Stay low, and let {npc} take the credit

effects.log: You keep quiet. "I blew on it all night," says {npc}, which is nearly true. Grandmother pats {his} head, which has never once happened before. {npc} looks at the jar, and you could swear {he} winks.

choices.text: Crackle, loudly, like a laugh

effects.log: A pop, a snap, a little burst of sparks. Grandmother jumps. {npc} bites {his} sleeve not to laugh. "The fire is laughing at me," says Grandmother, "in my own kitchen." Grandmother does not tell the neighbours that either.

events.text: Every morning {npc} lifts the lid of the jar, digs you out of your bed of ash with the iron tongs, and carries you to the stove on a bed of pine needles like a bowl of something hot. Every evening {he} brings you back and banks you, ash over the coals, lid on. {He} talks the whole time. About the dog, about the neighbours' child, about the rice, which is never enough. You are the only one in the house who listens to all of it.

choices.text: Listen to every word

effects.log: You learn the house from the inside of a jar: who owes rice to whom, which aunt cries in the well-house, why the dog limps. {npc} tells the fire everything. In nine generations, you suspect, nobody else ever did.

choices.text: Burn a little brighter on the cold mornings

effects.log: On the coldest mornings you make the stove roar in half the time. {npc} stops blowing on {his} fingers. The rice is cooked before Grandmother is up. Small things. They are the first things you ever gave.

choices.text: Hop off the tongs once, just to see

effects.log: You bounce off the tongs onto the earthen floor and roll under the rice chest. {npc} lies flat on {his} belly with a candle for a long time to find you. You are ashamed. A little. (-2 health)

events.text: A hard winter, and the woodpile is gone by the middle of it. The house burns pine needles and straw and the broken leg of a stool. One night there is nothing to bank you with but ash. {npc} sits by the cold jar in {his} padded jacket and whispers, "Please. Please. Just till morning." There is nothing in the jar to burn but you.

choices.text: Burn yourself till morning

effects.log: You burn on nothing, on your own small heat, all night. By dawn you are a speck. But you are a red speck, and {npc} feeds you a handful of straw at first light, and the fire of nine generations is ten. You sleep for three days. (-6 health)

choices.text: Shrink, and wait in the ash for wood

effects.log: You go so small and so slow that you are hardly fire at all, a warmth under the grey. {npc} thinks you have gone out and cries. At dawn {he} finds you still there. You learn that patience is also a way of burning.

choices.text: Call the wood: hop out and set the stool alight

effects.log: You jump out of the jar onto the last broken stool and it goes up with a whoosh. Warm. Too warm. {npc} beats out the edge of the straw mat with {his} hands. Nobody is hurt. But you burned a thing nobody gave you, and something in you notes it down. (Ash +1)

events.text: {npc} is grown now, and leaving: a match in a village over the pass, a new house, a new kitchen. On the last night {he} kneels by the fire jar, the way {he} did when {he} was small, and lifts the lid. "They have a fire," {he} says. "A perfectly good fire. I know." {He} does not put the lid back. {He} is holding a little clay pot.

choices.text: Hop into the pot

effects.log: Not you, not all of you: a coal of you, a red seed, which you drop into the pot like a gift. {npc} carries it over the pass in both hands and tips it into a new stove, and the new house is warm from the first night. There are two houses with your fire in them now. You are not sure, yet, what that means.

choices.text: Stay in the jar

effects.log: You stay where you were born. {npc} looks at you a long time, then nods, and puts the lid back with great care, the way {he} always did. In the morning {he} is gone. The new youngest of the house is four, and drops the tongs.

choices.text: Flare once, very bright, and then lie low

effects.log: One last flare, the whole jar red, {his} face red in it. "Yes," {he} says, "all right," as if you had said something. {He} goes over the pass without a coal. Every winter after that, they say, {his} kitchen is warmer than it has any right to be.

events.text: A breath comes down to you in the cold jar, so soft it is almost a question, and a pine needle is laid across you, and you eat it. That part is new. But the breath is not. Somewhere in the long dark before you there was a jar like this and a breath like this, and you were on the other side of it, kneeling, with frost on the paper door. You remember being the one who blew.

choices.text: Chirp

effects.log: A small, cross, perfectly clear chirp comes out of the ash. Whoever is kneeling at the jar jumps. So, in a way, do you. Some debts, it seems, are paid in the same coin, the other way round.

choices.text: Burn very gently, the way you were fed

effects.log: You come up slowly, carefully, a fire that knows what it is like to be afraid for a fire. By dawn the stove is lit. You keep a little of that fear in you always, and it makes you a better fire.

events.text: Somebody scoops you up out of the ash in their bare hands. It is a strange thing to be carried by someone who is being burned by you, and stranger still to know the burn from the inside: once, long ago, the hands were yours. There is a coin-sized place on your memory that is still warm on cold days.

choices.text: Make yourself as cool as you can

effects.log: You pull your heat into your middle, as small as a seed, for six steps. The hands that carry you are only reddened. It is the hardest thing you have ever done, and you are less than a year old.

choices.text: Burn, and remember what it cost

effects.log: You burn, because you are fire, and the hands do not let go, because they are hands like those. On the stove you shake out your heat and feel, somewhere, a scar. Not on them. On you. (-2 health)

events.text: A coal from another house is tipped into the cold jar beside you: borrowed fire, which the old people say must never be done. You know this. You know it from the wrong side: once you ran barefoot over a frozen yard for a coal like this one, and were scolded for it by noon. The borrowed coal glows. It is a good fire. It is not yours.

choices.text: Hop into it

effects.log: You hop into the borrowed coal and the whole jar flares red. Two fires, two houses, one flame. The old rule says it brings bad luck. You decide, there and then, that the old rule was written by someone who never had a neighbour.

choices.text: Stay beside it, your own small fire

effects.log: You sit beside the borrowed coal all night, two red points in a grey jar, and in the morning they have become one fire anyway, the way fires do. You learn that you will not always get to choose what you are part of.

events.text: The coldest week of the year, and the wind gets into the kitchen through every crack in the paper door. The jar is banked too thin tonight. You can feel the cold coming down through the ash toward you like water through sand.

choices.text: Burn hard all night

effects.log: You burn till dawn like a coal in a smith's forge. In the morning the jar is warm to the touch and the kitchen smells of you. You sleep through the whole next day. (-3 health)

choices.text: Draw in small and slow

effects.log: You go small, and slow, and deep in the ash, the way a frog sleeps in the mud. The cold passes over. In the morning you are still there. Fire, it turns out, can wait.

choices.text: Crackle until somebody wakes and banks you properly

effects.log: Pop. Snap. Pop. A light sleeper stumbles in, swears softly at the jar, and banks you properly, ash and a lid and a folded sack on top. Being looked after is a skill too.

events.text: On the clay shelf above the stove, where every dawn someone sets a white bowl of fresh water from the well, there is someone sitting. About the size of a pepper pot. Sooty from head to foot, with a sooty little beard and a sooty little hat, and very offended. "This," he says, pointing at the stove, "is MY fire. Has been for nine generations. And what, may I ask, do you think you are doing in it?"

choices.text: Tell him you are the fire

effects.log: "Nonsense," says the kitchen god. "I am the god of the fire. The fire does not talk back." You talk back. He sits down on the edge of the shelf with his legs dangling and looks at you for a long time. "Well," he says. "That is new."

choices.text: Bow, very low, as a guest bows

effects.log: You bow as low as a chick can bow, which is very low indeed, and topple over in the ash. The kitchen god is mollified. "Manners," he says. "At least somebody in this house has manners." He has not had a bow in years.

choices.text: Puff a little ash at him

effects.log: A small grey puff. The kitchen god coughs, and coughs, and sneezes into the bowl of clear water, which is a terrible thing to do to your own offering. He glares. You have made your first enemy among the gods, and he is the size of a pepper pot.

events.text: The kitchen god has drawn a line across the stove top in soot. "The left pot," he says, "is mine. The rice is mine. The soup is mine. You may have the right pot, the kettle, and anything that falls in the firebox." He folds his arms. "I am prepared to negotiate."

choices.text: Accept the right pot and the kettle

effects.log: You agree. He writes it on a scrap of paper in soot, and you put your claw-print on it, and he tucks it into his hat. The first treaty of your life. The kettle boils faster from then on, and the rice never burns.

choices.text: Ask for half the rice

ok.log: He argues. You argue. He says nine generations; you say you ARE the nine generations. In the end it is half the rice and all the scorched crust at the bottom of the pot, which he did not want anyway, and which is the best part.

fail.log: He laughs so hard his hat falls in the firebox. You get the kettle and the right pot and nothing else, and he takes his hat back out of you with great dignity. Still, a treaty is a treaty.

choices.text: Tell him a fire cannot be divided

effects.log: "Everything can be divided," says the kitchen god, "except a god's patience." He goes back up onto his shelf and does not speak to you for a season. The rice burns twice. Nobody knows why but the two of you.

events.text: At the year's end the kitchen god packs. A very small bundle on a very small stick. "I go up to report," he says, "on everything that happened in this house this year. Every quarrel, every curse, every foot put up on my stove." He looks at you sideways. "Every fire that played with the tongs."

choices.text: Ask him to report you kindly

effects.log: "Kindly," he says, "is not a thing I do." But when he comes back in the new year he brings you a grain of something from heaven, warm and bright, and says it was lying around. It was not lying around. (He reported you kindly.)

choices.text: Offer to carry him up yourself

effects.log: You are small. You get as far as the chimney top with a god on your back, and then the wind takes over, and the two of you tumble up into the cold sky, and he holds your neck feathers and shrieks the whole way. It is the first time you have been higher than the roof. He is never quite so stiff with you again.

choices.text: Tell him to report the truth

effects.log: "Hm," says the kitchen god. "The truth." He looks at you a while. "The truth is you kept the house warm in the hard winter. I suppose I shall have to put that in too." He goes up the chimney with his bundle. The house has a good year.

events.text: You are too big for the fire jar now, and too restless for the kitchen. The kitchen god knows it before you do. He sits on the edge of his shelf by the bowl of clear water with his sooty legs dangling and says, without looking at you, "So. Off you go, then. They all go, the ones that grow."

choices.text: Promise to come back at every year's end

effects.log: "Hm," he says. "Promises." But you see him, later, draw a little bird in the soot at the end of his shelf, where nobody but a fire would see it. You come back. Not every year. Often enough.

choices.text: Leave him a coal of your own, on the shelf

effects.log: One small coal, set by the bowl of water, where it should not be able to burn and does, for years. The kitchen god warms his hands at it on winter nights and pretends it is his own idea.

choices.text: Just go, the way fire goes

effects.log: Up the flue, out of the chimney, into the morning. You do not look back. Behind you, on a sooty shelf, a god the size of a pepper pot says something very rude and blows his nose. It is the closest thing to a blessing he knows.

events.text: The problem with being an ash-grey chick in a kitchen is that the kitchen is full of ash. You sit in it and you are it. The cat walks past you. The dog sniffs you and sneezes. Grandmother rests the hot pot on you, briefly, before you object.

choices.text: Object loudly

effects.log: You object in a voice like a tea kettle. Grandmother lifts the pot, looks at the patch of ash that complained, and says nothing whatever for the rest of the morning. (-2 health)

choices.text: Learn to be ash when it suits you

effects.log: If you can be mistaken for ash, then you can be ash. You practise: still, grey, cool on top and hot underneath. By the end of the winter the cat walks over you without noticing. It is the most useful thing you learn this year.

choices.text: Sit on the clean stove-top instead, where you show

effects.log: You sit on the stove where everyone can see you: a grey lump on the black iron. "Oh, look," says someone, "the stove is moulting." It is not the dignity you wanted. But nobody puts a pot on you.

events.text: Ash day. Once a season the whole firebox is raked out with the long iron, and all the old ash goes into a basket, and the basket goes out to the field for the soil. You are asleep in the firebox when the rake comes in.

choices.text: Wake, and hop up onto the rake

effects.log: You ride the rake out of the firebox like a boat out of a harbour and sit on the end of it, blinking. The one holding the rake goes very still. Then, carefully, they set the rake down and back out of the kitchen. You are a story in the village by noon.

choices.text: Dig down, deep, and stay

effects.log: You dig in under the back stones where the rake cannot reach. It scrapes past you, again and again. Then quiet. You come out into a clean, cold, empty firebox, and it is the loneliest place in the world until someone lights it. (-2 health)

choices.text: Go out with the ash, and see the field

effects.log: Out in the basket, out on the furrows, out under a sky so big you fall over. You warm the soil you land in until a little ring of green comes up there out of season. Somebody small comes to find you before dark.

events.text: A new hearth brush, stiff straw, and a new pair of hands on it: a cousin come to help for the winter who has never heard of you. Sweep, sweep, sweep, the whole floor toward the door and out into the snow, and you in the middle of the pile, rolling.

choices.text: Ride the pile out into the snow and try to fly

ok.log: Out the door, over the step, and you open your stubby wings and for one moment the pile goes on without you. You land in the snow and hiss, and steam, and walk back into the kitchen past the cousin, who sits down.

fail.log: Out the door and into a snowdrift, which is the worst place in the world for you to be. You are a hiss of steam in a hole of slush by the time a small pair of hands digs you out. You do not stop shivering for a week. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lie still and let it happen

effects.log: Out into the yard with the rest of the ash. You lie there in the cold until somebody small comes running in a panic and turns over every grey lump in the yard to find you. It takes a while. It is worth the wait.

choices.text: Burn a hole in the brush

effects.log: The straw catches. The cousin drops the brush, stamps on it, and runs out shouting about a fire spirit. Grandmother comes in, looks at you sitting on the scorched floor, and says, "Yes. That is the fire spirit. Leave it alone." (Ash +1)

events.text: After the business with the cousin and the hearth brush, {npc} takes no chances. {He} carries you in the long sleeve of {his} padded jacket, everywhere: to the well, to the fields, to the village school where {he} sits at the back and recites the Thousand Character Classic with one arm held very carefully away from {his} body.

choices.text: Ride in the sleeve and listen to the lessons

effects.log: "Heaven is dark, earth is yellow." You learn the first lines before {npc} does, and hum them back through the cotton. {He} gets them right on the first try for once. The teacher is amazed. The sleeve is warm.

choices.text: Keep {npc} warm through the whole winter

effects.log: The coldest winter in years, and {npc} has no chilblains. Not one. The other children compare raw red hands at the school door, and {npc} keeps {his} arm by {his} side and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Scorch the sleeve, a little, to get out

effects.log: A small brown burn on the cuff, and you tumble out into the dust of the schoolyard. {npc} scoops you up, scolds you in a whisper, and puts you back. The burn stays on the sleeve for years. {He} never mends it.

events.text: Somebody is stealing from the fire jar. Every night a coal goes missing, a good red one, and every morning there is a tiny trail of ash leading to a gap in the floorboards by the rice chest. Somebody under the floor is very warm this winter at your expense.

choices.text: Follow the trail under the floor

effects.log: Down through the gap, into the dark, along the joists to a nest of straw and rags with a red coal glowing in the middle of it like an egg. And sitting on it, warming her belly, a large brown rat with eight blind pink babies. She looks at you. You look at her.

choices.text: Lie in wait in the jar

effects.log: At midnight a whiskered nose lifts the edge of the ash. You bite it. There is a squeal, and a scrabble, and a large brown rat sits on the kitchen floor holding its nose, and glares at you, and says, in rat, "That was uncalled for."

events.text: The rat comes back for her coal, and this time she has brought her husband, who is twice her size and missing an ear. They sit on the rim of the fire jar, one on each side, and look down at you, a grey chick half the size of either of them.

choices.text: Fight them for the jar

ok.log: You come up out of the ash like a struck match. Singed whiskers, a squeal, two rats going over the rim backwards. They do not come back for a month. When they do, they come with great respect, and from the far side of the kitchen.

fail.log: One-Ear gets you by the wing and shakes you like a rag. You burn his mouth and he lets go, but your wing is wrong for a season and the coal goes under the floor anyway. (-12 health)
fail.deathCause: the rats under the kitchen floor

choices.text: Offer them the cooling coals at dawn

effects.log: "Not the red ones," you tell them. "The grey ones, at dawn, when the stove is lit. They stay warm till noon." The rats confer. One-Ear says it is a trick. His wife says she has eight children and a cold floor. It is not a trick. It is your second treaty.

choices.text: Puff yourself up and burn white

effects.log: For one breath you are as hot as a smith's coal, a white point in a grey jar. Both rats go backwards off the rim. It costs you, and you lie in the ash for two days after, dim and sore, but they do not come back that winter. (-3 health)

events.text: The cat of the house has learned there are rats under the floor. Every night now she sits by the gap at the rice chest, still as a jar, waiting. Underneath, you can hear eight small rats, not blind any more, breathing.

choices.text: Warn the rats

effects.log: You drop down the gap and tell them, in the little sounds, which way the cat is facing. They go out the other side, under the wall, all of them, in a long brown line. The cat waits by the gap for a week. One-Ear sends you, in thanks, a single grain of rice.

choices.text: Let the cat do as cats do

effects.log: You stay in the jar. The cat is a cat. In the morning there are seven rats under the floor, and the coals go missing again, one a night, out of grief or habit. You decide you are not sorry, and are not sure.

choices.text: Sit by the gap yourself, glowing, so the cat will not

effects.log: The cat does not like you. She does not like anything hot that looks back. She sits at a distance and twitches her tail, and you sit by the gap all night, and the rats under the floor have a quiet winter. (-2 health)

events.text: Years on, and there are rats in every wall of the village, and every one of them, somehow, knows about you. They leave you things. A bright button. A dried jujube. The good crust of a rice cake. One spring a very old rat with one ear comes out into the middle of the kitchen floor in daylight, which no rat does, and sits there.

choices.text: Go down and sit with him

effects.log: He is old, very old for a rat, and cold. You sit beside him on the floor until he is warm, and he goes back under the boards, slowly, and does not come out again. The next morning there are seven bright buttons in a row by the fire jar.

choices.text: Ask the rats what they hear in the walls

effects.log: Everything. Who hides rice, who hides coins, who weeps, who plots. The rats of the village tell you all of it in exchange for warm ash at dawn. Swallows under the eaves, rats in the walls: a fire, you learn, should know what is happening in its house.

events.text: The jar platform: a raised bed of stones in the yard, and on it the house's great brown jars of soy sauce and bean paste and pepper paste, each with its lid, each older than Grandmother. They are the highest things you can see from the kitchen door. You have decided to fly to them.

choices.text: Run and jump

ok.log: Run, flap, flap, flap, and you land on the lid of the soy jar with a clack. You did it. You sit there, grey and enormous and pleased, until the lid tips and you go into the soy sauce. (You did it.)

fail.log: Run, flap, and you land on the stones between the jars and roll into a pepper paste jar's shadow. A small hand lifts you out. You are dusty and hurt and you will try again tomorrow. (-3 health)

choices.text: Climb the woodpile first, and glide

effects.log: Up the woodpile, claw over claw, and off the top in a long falling hop that ends exactly on the lid of the bean paste jar. Glide, not fly. But it is the first time the air has carried you anywhere. You remember the feeling all night.

events.text: Off the jar lids and into everything that smells of beans and salt, and now you are a sticky, salty, steaming grey lump that smells like a feast, and every dog in the lane knows it. The persimmon tree by the wall is the next thing up. Its lowest branch is two lengths of you above the jar lids.

choices.text: Climb the bark like a woodpecker

effects.log: Claw, beak, claw, and a little scorch mark on the bark at every hold. You reach the branch and sit on it among the orange persimmons, panting. The tree has a ladder of burns up its trunk for the rest of its life. The children of the house call them your stairs.

choices.text: Jump from the jar lid, wings open

ok.log: Jump, flap, and a branch is under your feet, swaying. You flew. Up. Upward is a different thing from not falling. You sit in the persimmon tree till dusk, in love with the word.

fail.log: Jump, flap, and a persimmon, an over-ripe one, which bursts. You go down with it into the dog's bowl. The dog is very interested. (-4 health)

events.text: From the persimmon tree, the roof. Thatch, gold-grey, steep, and above it the ridge: the line where the house ends and the sky begins. The wind comes up the slope of the roof warm from the kitchen chimney. It smells like home. It is lifting the loose straw at the edge, and it could lift you.

choices.text: Ride the chimney's warm wind up to the ridge

ok.log: You open your wings over the chimney and the warm smoke takes you, up, up, past the thatch, and puts you on the ridge-pole like a hand setting down a cup. The whole village is below you, and the paddies, and the hills, and a long way off, the shine of the southern sea. You flew. (Your first flight: the stage need is met.)

fail.log: The smoke takes you, turns you over, and drops you down the far side of the roof into the vegetable patch. Cabbages. A whole row of cabbages, flattened, and one of them slightly cooked. (-4 health)

choices.text: Flap the whole way up on your own wings

ok.log: Flap, flap, flap, the thatch going by, the ridge coming down to meet you, and you land on it all at once and nearly go over the other side. You flew, on nothing but yourself. (Your first flight: the stage need is met.)

fail.log: Halfway up the thatch your wings give out and you slide all the way down to the eaves on your back, with straw in your beak. A small face looks up at you from the yard and does not laugh, quite. (-5 health)

choices.text: Not today: sit in the tree and watch the wind

effects.log: You watch how the smoke goes up, where it curls, where the straw lifts. Tomorrow, or the day after. Fire is in no hurry when it is learning a thing.

events.text: Dawn on a still day, and the chimney smoke is going straight up, a grey rope from the kitchen to the sky. You have fallen off the roof, the tree and the woodpile more times than you will admit. The children of the house have started counting. Today, you decide, you go up the rope.

choices.text: Up the smoke, straight up

effects.log: You climb the smoke the way you climbed the persimmon bark, wingbeat over wingbeat, and come out of the top of it above the roof, above the tree, above everything, and the smoke goes on up without you and you are flying. Not falling. Flying. You land on the ridge as if you had done it every day of your life. (Your first flight: the stage need is met.)

choices.text: Go up the thatch, slowly, claw by claw, then leap

effects.log: Claw by claw to the ridge, and then, from the very top, you jump the other way, out over the lane, and the air holds. It holds! You go round the house twice before you remember how to land, and land on the jar lids, and do not fall in. (Your first flight: the stage need is met.)

events.text: You fly most mornings now, a grey streak from the chimney to the persimmon tree to the ridge and back, and the village has stopped looking up. Except the children. The children of the lane have a game: whoever sees the grey bird first in the morning gets the first rice cake. They shout when they see you. "There! There!"

choices.text: Fly low over them, so they all win

effects.log: You go along the lane at the height of a child's head, and every child shouts "There!" at once, and nobody can say who saw you first, and the game falls apart in an argument. It is the best morning of the year.

choices.text: Hide, and let them look

effects.log: You sit in the persimmon tree, grey among grey branches, and they search the sky for an hour. The smallest one finds you, finally, by the little curl of heat above your head. Clever. You make a note of that child.

events.text: A newcomer in the house: {npc}, married in this spring from a village down the valley, the newest member of the household, and so, by the custom of the house, the keeper of the fire from now on. Grandmother shows {him} the jar, the tongs, the banking, the lid. "Nine generations," says Grandmother. "It has never gone out." You are asleep in the ash, and very hungry. You are growing, and growing takes embers.

choices.text: Eat a few coals in the night, as usual

effects.log: You eat the red ones, the best ones, until the jar is nearly grey. You leave enough to light the stove. Just enough. You think.

choices.text: Eat only the grey ones, carefully

effects.log: You eat the cooling, half-grey ones and leave the red, and in the morning the jar is fine, and you are still hungry. A growing fire cannot live on leftovers for long. You know it, and are sorry already.

events.text: The fire is out. Again. Third morning in a month. {npc} kneels at the jar in the grey dawn with {his} face very white, and Grandmother stands over {him}, and says the things grandmothers say: careless, lazy, a bad sign, a house that loses its fire loses its luck. {npc} says nothing at all. You are sitting very small and very full behind the jar, where the last red coal went.

choices.text: Go back into the jar and light yourself up

effects.log: You hop in and burn red, and Grandmother stops mid-word. "Well," says Grandmother, "it was not out, then." {npc} looks at the jar, and then, slowly, past it, at the small shape behind it. {He} says nothing. But {he} knows.

choices.text: Stay hidden, and be ashamed

effects.log: You stay where you are. {npc} borrows fire from the neighbours, which must never be done, and takes the scolding for that too. You feel it like a coal in your crop. You eat nothing the next night. (Smoulder +2)

events.text: {npc} sits up. All night, by the fire jar, in the dark, with a stick across {his} knees and {his} eyes wide open, the way the old stories say you must when something is putting out your fire. Near dawn you cannot bear it any longer: you are so hungry. You creep to the jar. {npc} does not move. But as you dive into the coals, something fine and soft catches on your tail feathers: a red silk thread, from the needle in {his} hand.

choices.text: Bolt out of the kitchen with the thread trailing

effects.log: Out the door, over the yard, over the wall, up the hill, the thread paying out behind you from the spool in {npc}'s lap. You stop in the pines above the village, tangled, a grey chick on a red string. Below, a lamp is lit. Someone is coming up the hill, winding the thread as {he} comes.

choices.text: Stop, turn round, and look at {him}

effects.log: You stand in the jar with the thread on your tail and look at {npc}. {npc} looks at you. It is the longest look of your life. Then {he} says, very quietly, "Oh. You are hungry." And {he} gets up and fetches you the good coals from the stove.

events.text: The thread runs up the hill, through the pines, to a hollow under an old oak where you fell and tangled. {npc} follows it with a lamp and finds you. And beside you, where your heat has thawed a patch of the frozen leaf litter, a plant with five leaves on a long stem and a cluster of red berries: wild ginseng, old and fat, the kind that is dug once in a lifetime.

choices.text: Scratch at the root, so {he} sees

mem.note: led me to the ginseng with your fire

effects.log: {npc} digs with {his} fingers all morning so as not to break a hair of the root. It is as long as a forearm and shaped like a little person. It pays the family's debts and then some. From that day nobody in the house says a word against the keeper of the fire, and the keeper of the fire leaves a little dish of good coals by the jar every night.

choices.text: Lie down on it and keep it secret

effects.log: You spread your grey wings over the five leaves. {npc} looks at the plant, and at you, and leaves it. "Yours," {he} says. "I only wanted to know who was eating my fire." It is still there, under the oak, years later, when you come back to look.

choices.text: Burn off the thread and fly

effects.log: A flick of heat and the thread falls away and you are gone into the dark. {npc} stands in the hollow with the lamp and the empty thread, and does not see the ginseng at {his} feet. In the morning the fire jar is full and red. You have decided to eat less. You do not manage it.

events.text: {npc} is the one the house turns to now. Grandmother is gone, and {npc} has grey in {his} hair, and keeps the fire, and keeps the keys, and on the coldest night of the year {he} sits down by the jar with the newest member of the house, a scared young thing married in this spring, and hands {him} the tongs. "Nine generations," {npc} says. "Ten, now. If it goes out some morning, you come and tell me first." And {he} looks, just once, at you.

choices.text: Burn bright for the new keeper

effects.log: You burn up red and steady and friendly, the best fire the new one has ever seen. {npc} smiles into {his} sleeve. Some things in a house are handed down in words. Some are handed down in a look at the fire jar.

choices.text: Chirp at {npc}, once, like old times

effects.log: A small clear chirp from the jar. The new one jumps out of {his} skin. {npc} laughs out loud, for the first time in a long time. "The fire talks," {he} says. "You will get used to it."

events.text: Runners from the county office, in black hats, at the gate of the great house at the head of the village where you have taken to sleeping in the kitchen: they carry a lidded brazier of new fire, rubbed from apricot and jujube wood at the start of summer by order of the court, and a paper with a seal on it. Old fire, the paper says, grows fierce; it breeds fevers and quarrels; it must be put out and the season's new fire taken in. "All of it," says the runner, looking at the fire jar. "The old fire goes out today."

choices.text: Listen to the reasons on the paper

effects.log: The runner reads it aloud for the cook, who cannot read: elm and willow in spring, apricot and jujube in summer, mulberry in the late summer, oak in autumn, and in winter the hard woods. Fire kept too long exceeds its measure. You sit in the jar and think: so that is what I am going to have to do. Every fire. Every season. For ever.

choices.text: Hiss at the runner from the jar

effects.log: A long hiss, like water on a stove. The runner takes a step back and looks at the cook. The cook looks at the ceiling. "Old jar," says the cook. "Cracks." (Smoulder +2)

events.text: They tip the old fire jar out in the yard and pour water on it. On you. The new fire, apricot and jujube, is carried into the kitchen like a bride in a palanquin, and the cook bows to it, and the runners watch. You are a red sparrow in a puddle of black slush behind the woodpile, and very angry, and the old fire was nine generations old if you count the house you came from, and nobody asked you.

choices.text: Hide in the woodpile until they go

effects.log: You dry yourself on your own heat in the dark between the logs, and when the runners have gone you go back into the kitchen and sit on the new fire's stove like a lodger who was there first. The new fire does not mind. It is young. It does not know anything.

choices.text: Go into the new fire and become part of it

effects.log: You walk into the new fire in the stove, apricot and jujube, clean and bright, and it takes you the way a river takes a stream. You come out of the other side lighter. Something old and heavy has burned off you that you did not know was there. So that is what the paper meant.

choices.text: Argue with the clerk

ok.log: You perch on the brazier and tell the clerk exactly what you think, in a voice like a kettle. The clerk listens to the whole thing, nods, and writes on the back of the paper: "Old fire found to be in good order; a bird of some kind." That is the first time you appear in any record.

fail.log: You perch on the brazier and tell the clerk what you think. The clerk hears a sparrow screeching, and swats at it with the paper, and you fall in the slush again. Arguing with clerks, you learn, is harder than arguing with gods. (-4 health)

events.text: Some time later the cook of the great house falls ill with a summer fever, and two of the kitchen boys quarrel and one cuts the other, and the old housekeeper says it is because of the new fire, and the young steward says it is because of the old one. Everybody in the kitchen is arguing about fire. Nobody asks the fire.

choices.text: Sit in the stove and burn gently, the whole season

effects.log: You keep the stove low and clean and steady, no roaring, no smoke, a fire with good manners. The cook recovers. The kitchen boys make it up over a burnt rice crust. The housekeeper says the new fire has settled. Nobody looks at you, which is as it should be.

choices.text: Watch which fire the fevers follow

effects.log: You watch all summer. It is not the new fire and it is not the old one: it is the bad well behind the stables. But the watching teaches you to feel when a fire is too old, the way a fever is felt in a forehead. You will need that.

events.text: Summer again, and the runners again, with the brazier and the paper and the apricot and jujube. This time you are waiting for them on the gatepost. The runner who read the paper that first time sees you, and stops, and looks at you for a long time. He is older than he was. "You," he says. "The red bird of the great house kitchen."

choices.text: Fly down and walk into the brazier

effects.log: You hop down into the new fire before anyone can stop you and sit in it, red in the red. The runner does not drop the brazier. He carries it in to the kitchen with you in it, very carefully, and bows to the stove after he sets it down, which is not in the rite at all.

choices.text: Ask him, in your way, where the wood comes from

effects.log: He does not understand birds, but he understands a bird looking at a bundle of sticks. "Apricot," he says, holding one up. "Jujube." He shows you how the board is notched and the drill is spun until the dust smokes. You watch the new fire born from nothing but wood and patience. It is not so different from you.

events.text: The widow's Hearth, the first fire you ever gave, has been burning a few years now, and something in it feels older than it should: a tightness, a heat that is too eager. It is the start of summer. Up at the great house the runners are carrying in the new fire. You think of the bundle of apricot and jujube on the runner's back.

choices.text: Steal a sprig of apricot and jujube and renew the Hearth

effects.log: One sprig of each from the runner's bundle while he drinks at the well. You fly them to the widow's stove and rub them together with beak and claw until the dust smokes, and catch the new flame, and give the old fire into it. The Hearth burns clean and young again. Your first renewal. There will be a great many. (The Hearth is renewed.)

choices.text: Leave it: it is still young

effects.log: It is only a few years old. You leave it, and make a note in the part of you that keeps such notes: the Hearth, lit in the hard week of winter, a little eager. One day it will need the season's wood. Not yet.

events.text: Red feathers, coming in at last, at the tips, and the sparrows of the paddies think you are one of them. A sparrow with a sunburn. "Too long in the sun," says a fat old sparrow on the dyke, kindly, and offers you a seat on the fence and half a grasshopper. "Happens to the best of us. Sit in the shade a bit."

choices.text: Sit on the fence and be a sparrow for a while

effects.log: You sit with them in a row on the fence, all puffed up against the wind, and they tell you about grain, and cats, and boys with slings, and which farmer's wife throws out the rice crust. Nobody has ever just let you sit in a row before. It is wonderful.

choices.text: Tell them you are a fire

effects.log: "Of course you are, dear," says the old sparrow. "We all are, a bit, at your age." The others nod. Sparrows, you learn, believe anything and are surprised by nothing. You are a fire. They let you sit on the fence anyway.

choices.text: Puff up and show your red

effects.log: You fluff out every red feather you have, which is about nine. The sparrows are impressed for nearly a breath, then go back to arguing about a grasshopper. You are less impressive than you hoped. (Smoulder +1)

events.text: Autumn, and the rice is gold and heavy and bowing to the water, and the flock goes down into it every morning like rain going up. The farmers hate it. You have never eaten rice from the stalk. The flock is calling you down into the warm, rustling gold.

choices.text: Go down with the flock and eat

effects.log: Sweet, milky, warm from the sun. You eat until you are round. You understand, now, why the sparrows put up with the boys and the slings and the cats. It is worth it. It is entirely worth it.

choices.text: Stay on the fence and watch the farmers

effects.log: Every grain the flock eats is a grain a family does not. You can see it in the farmer's face. You stay on the fence and eat grasshoppers, and the old sparrow calls you a strange bird, which is fair.

choices.text: Warm the paddy so it ripens faster, ahead of the flock

effects.log: You sit in the middle of one farmer's paddy all week and give it summer. It ripens three days ahead of the rest and is cut before the flock comes. The farmer thinks he is lucky. He is.

events.text: The children of the village are out on the dykes with wooden clappers and tin pans, as they are every autumn, shouting "hwoi, hwoi" until the paddies ring, and the flock goes up and down and up again like a shaken blanket. One small child has a sling, and is good with it.

choices.text: Lead the flock away to the stubble on the hill

effects.log: You go up and away, red at the front, and the flock follows the odd bird with the sunburn, over the hill to a field already cut where the gleanings lie thick. The children cheer. The sparrows eat. Everybody wins but the child with the sling.

choices.text: Dodge the sling stones for the joy of it

ok.log: Left, right, up, a stone whistling under you, a stone whistling over. The child is very good. You are better. By noon the whole dyke is watching the duel, and when you land on the child's own clapper at the end, the child laughs, and lowers the sling.

fail.log: The fourth stone catches your wing. You come down in the mud of a paddy and hiss until the water steams round you, and the child runs away screaming that the sparrow is on fire. (-6 health)

choices.text: Sit on the scarecrow and glare

effects.log: You sit on the scarecrow's straw hat and glare at the children, who glare back. Stalemate. The scarecrow is no help. Scarecrows never are.

events.text: The farmer has dressed the scarecrow in his own old hemp jacket and a broken straw hat, and the flock has learned it in a day, the way sparrows do: the old sparrow is asleep on its shoulder. You land on its arm to join her, and the straw under your feet is very dry, and it is very hot today, and you are angrier than you knew about the children and their sling. The sleeve begins, quietly, to smoke.

choices.text: Swallow the anger and pinch out the smoke

effects.log: You pull the heat back into your own breast, all of it, and it sits there like a hot stone. The sleeve stops smoking. Nobody knows. You carry the stone home and sit with it all night. (Smoulder +3, -2 health)

choices.text: Fly off before it catches

effects.log: You get off the scarecrow and up into the clean sky, and the smoke stops when you go. Sometimes the answer to a temper is distance. Not always. Today.

choices.text: Let it burn

effects.log: The sleeve goes up, then the jacket, then the hat, and the flock bursts off it like sparks, and the scarecrow stands burning in the gold paddy at noon like a torch. The fire does not spread; the paddy is wet. But the farmer's jacket is gone, and the village talks about a burning sparrow all winter, and the old sparrow will not sit near you again. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Swallow it, and fail

effects.log: You try to pull it back in. There is no room left. The heat goes out of you on its own, the sleeve and the hat go up, and you have swallowed and burned both at once, the worst of both. (Smoulder +3, Ash +1, -2 health)

events.text: The old sparrow is very old now, for a sparrow, which is not old at all. She sits on the fence in the first frost with her feathers puffed out and does not go down into the stubble with the others. "Strange bird," she says, when you sit beside her. "Warm, though. You always were warm."

choices.text: Sit against her all winter

effects.log: You sit on the fence against her all winter, a red bird and a brown one, and she does not feel the frost once. In spring she does not wake. The flock does not mourn the way people do. You do, a little, the way fire does: by burning lower for a while.

choices.text: Ask her what she thinks you are

effects.log: "A sparrow who will not stay a sparrow," she says. "We get them sometimes. They go off and become something. Herons. Kingfishers. The odd hawk." She closes her eyes. "Do not become a hawk, dear." You promise.

events.text: At the bottom of the lane, below the great house, there is a house with no smoke. Every chimney in the village breathes at dusk, grey and slow, and that one does not. In the hardest week of winter you sit on its broken fence and look through the gap in the paper door. An old widow, {npc}, in a patched jacket, eating cold millet with {his} hands wrapped in rags. The stove is stone-cold. There has been no wood for a month.

choices.text: Watch {him} through the night

effects.log: {npc} eats, washes the bowl in cold water, lies down in all {his} clothes, and does not sleep. Neither do you. At dawn {he} goes out with a basket to scrape for twigs in the frozen woods, and comes back with almost nothing.

choices.text: Sit on {his} cold chimney all night, as warm as you can

effects.log: You sit on the chimney pot and burn into the clay all night. A little warmth goes down the flue into the floor. Not much. {npc} sleeps, for the first time in days, curled on the one warm patch. (-3 health)

events.text: You have decided. A coal from the great house's stove, the good apricot-and-jujube fire, carried across the village in your beak to {npc}'s cold kitchen. It is a long way for a red sparrow with a coal in its mouth. The coal is very hot. Your tongue already knows it.

choices.text: Carry it straight across, the short way

ok.log: Over the great house wall, over the lane, over the well, the coal burning your tongue the whole way, and you do not drop it. You set it down on the widow's doorstep, sizzling. Your tongue will be burnt for a month. (-4 health)

fail.log: Halfway over the well the pain is too much and you open your beak, and the coal goes down the well with a hiss. You sit on the well rim with your tongue out for an hour. Tomorrow. Tomorrow, and a smaller coal. (-6 health)

choices.text: Carry it the long way, by the hedges, out of the wind

effects.log: Hedge to hedge, wall to wall, resting the coal on stones while your tongue cools. It takes all afternoon. The coal is a little smaller by the end, and so are you. But it is still red when you get there. (-3 health)

events.text: The hardest week of the winter. The wind comes down off the hills with snow in it, and the old people of the village do not get up in the mornings. {npc} has burned the fence, and the door of the woodshed, and now there is nothing. {He} sits by the cold stove in the dark with {his} hands under {his} arms, and says, to nobody, "Well. This is how it goes, then."

choices.text: Fly in through the gap in the paper door

effects.log: You come in out of the snow, red and steaming, and sit on the cold stove. {npc} looks at you for a long time. "A sparrow," {he} says. "A red sparrow. Well. You are warmer than I am." {He} holds out {his} hands to you, the way one does to a fire.

choices.text: Go for the coal now, through the snow

effects.log: Out into the snow, which is the worst place in the world for you, over to the great house, back with a coal. You are a hiss of steam with wings by the time you reach the widow's door. It is still red. Just. (-3 health)

events.text: One more coal from the great house in your beak, the widow's cold stove in front of you, the kindling {npc} laid in it a month ago and never lit. You drop the coal. It sits on the straw. It goes dull. It is going out, and you have nothing left to give it but yourself.

choices.text: Breathe on it, the way you were once breathed on

mem.note: lit my stove in the hardest winter

effects.log: You breathe on it as softly as the youngest of your house once breathed on you, and the straw takes, and the twigs take, and the stove roars. {npc} sits down on the floor in front of it and cries. The first warm night in that house in a month. The Hearth is lit, and it is the first fire you ever gave. (The Hearth burns: the stage need is met.)

choices.text: Give it a coal of your own breast

mem.note: lit my stove in the hardest winter

effects.log: You open your beak over the stove and something comes out of you that is not the great house's coal: a red seed of your own fire. It hurts like losing a feather from the inside. The stove goes up red and gold. {npc} holds {his} hands to it and laughs, and coughs, and laughs. The Hearth is lit, and it is the first fire you ever gave. (-6 health; the Hearth burns: the stage need is met.)

events.text: The widow's kitchen has smoke every dusk now, grey and slow like everyone else's. {npc} keeps the fire the way the old people did, banked in a cracked jar every night, and talks to it. You sit on the fence and listen. "Good evening," {he} says to the fire. "It was cold today. You did well." And once, not looking up at the fence: "Thank you, little red one."

choices.text: Come down and sit by the stove with {him}

effects.log: You sit on the stove lip and {npc} sits on the floor and you both look at the fire. {He} tells it about {his} husband, who was a fool and a good man, and about a son who went to the coast and never wrote. The fire listens. So do you. It is a good evening.

choices.text: Stay on the fence, a little shy

effects.log: You do not come down. You do not have to. {npc} leaves a pinch of millet on the fence post every morning after that, and you eat it, and both of you pretend not to know who left it.

events.text: You had already given your first fire before you ever saw this house: a Hearth for a cold kitchen elsewhere in the valley. But here is the widow, {npc}, cold, and here are you, with the great house's stove a lane away. The Hearth is one fire. Warmth is not a thing you can only give once.

choices.text: Carry {him} coals every night of the hard week

effects.log: A coal a night, seven nights, across the lane in your beak. Not a fire of yours, only warmth, borrowed and given. {npc} survives the winter. In spring {he} puts out a dish of millet on the fence post, and it is there every morning after. (-4 health)

choices.text: Lead the youngest of the great house to {his} door with a basket of wood

effects.log: You fly in circles round the head of the great house's smallest kitchen child until the child follows you, scolding, down the lane, and sees the cold house, and runs back for wood without being asked. Some fires you give. Some you only point at.

events.text: The longest night of the year, and the whole village has cooked red-bean porridge, dark and sweet, with little white rice balls in it, one for every year of your age. Before anybody eats, the grandmothers go out with ladles and fling it on the gates, the walls, the posts of the cowshed: red, because red drives off the ghosts. You are sitting on the great house's gate when the first ladle comes.

choices.text: Stay put

effects.log: Splat. Warm, sweet, sticky, everywhere. You sit on the gate dripping porridge and blinking, and the grandmother with the ladle looks at you for a long moment and says, "Well. That one will not be troubled by ghosts." You spend the evening cleaning your feathers. It tastes very good.

choices.text: Dodge, and eat what lands on the wall

effects.log: You hop aside, and the porridge hits the wall where you were, and you eat it off the wall, and nobody seems to mind. You are red; the porridge is red. The grandmother decides it is all part of the same custom.

choices.text: Ask the ghosts, quietly, whether it works

effects.log: There is a thin grey shape by the well that nobody else sees. It looks at the porridge on the gate and shudders, and goes off up the lane to a house that did not cook any. It works. Red works. You think about that for a long time.

events.text: A red bird on the gate on the longest night, they are saying in the village. Covered in porridge and did not fly off. A sign. A good sign. Red on the solstice: the year turns, the light comes back. By the next solstice there is a little dish of porridge left out on the gatepost specially, and a crowd of children waiting to see if you come.

choices.text: Come, and eat it in front of them

effects.log: You land on the gatepost and eat the whole dish, rice balls and all, while twenty children hold their breath. Then you fly round the village once, low, red against the snow. The children say the year will be lucky. It is, more or less, which is all anyone can ask of a year.

choices.text: Do not come: you are not a sign

effects.log: You stay on a fence out of sight that night, out of sight. The children wait, and go home, and say the sign did not come, and are not lucky or unlucky. You do not want to be a sign. Signs are what people look at instead of each other.

events.text: The solstice again, and the dish on the gatepost again, and the children again. But there is a new child among them, sick, wrapped in a quilt in a neighbour's arms, carried out because the family hoped the red bird would come. The child has a fever that has gone on all winter.

choices.text: Land on the quilt, and warm the child

effects.log: You sit on the quilt over the child's chest and give it all the warmth you have, slow and even, the way you bank a jar. The fever breaks by the new year. Whether it was you, you will never know. Neither will they. It is a good thing not to know.

choices.text: Eat the porridge and fly round the house three times

effects.log: You do what they hoped: the porridge, the three circles, red against the snow. The child laughs, the first time all winter. Fevers are fevers. Laughing is something too.

events.text: The first full moon of the year, and every child in the village is on the paddy dykes with a fire can: an old tin punched full of holes, a few coals inside, on a long string, whirled round and round until it roars. The grown-ups burn the dykes for the rats and the bugs and the bad luck, and the whole valley is drawn in lines of fire. You have never seen so much fire you did not light.

choices.text: Fly the dykes and keep every line in its place

effects.log: Up and down the dykes all night, nudging a flame back from a haystack here, a woodpile there. Nobody sees you. The fires stay where they are told. It is the first time you understand that keeping a fire and minding it are not the same thing.

choices.text: Ride a fire can as it whirls

ok.log: You hop onto a whirling can and ride it round and round, a red bird in a wheel of sparks, and the child swinging it shrieks with joy and does not let go. It is the most fun you have ever had in your life.

fail.log: You hop onto a whirling can and are flung off it into the next paddy, which is frozen. You go through the ice. A hiss, a cloud of steam, a very wet red bird. (-5 health)

events.text: A string snaps. A fire can goes sailing up off the dyke, trailing sparks like a comet, over the dark, and comes down with a thump on the thatched roof of the widow Seo's house at the edge of the paddies. The thatch begins to smoke. It is dry. It is the end of winter. Everything is dry.

choices.text: Call the fire home

effects.log: You land on the roof and call it, the way you would call your own: come here. Come back. And it comes, every spark of it, out of the thatch and into your breast, hot and furious and then quiet. The smoke stops. The first fire you ever called home was not even yours.

choices.text: Beat it out with your wings

effects.log: You beat at the smouldering ring with your wings until the sparks are dead and your feathers are singed. It works. It hurts. A fire bird putting out a fire with its own body is not a dignified thing, and nobody saw it, which is the only mercy. (-5 health)

choices.text: Let it burn a moment, and shout for the village

effects.log: You screech like a kettle until doors open, and the village runs with buckets, and the roof is out by the third bucket. But a corner of it burned first, a black bite out of the widow Seo's thatch, and you watched it. (Ash +1)

events.text: The first full moon again, the fire cans again, and this year the headman has made the children tie their strings double, and stationed a grandmother with a bucket by every thatched house. On the widow Seo's roof, someone has set a little dish of rice cake by the ridge. It is for you.

choices.text: Eat it, and keep watch from her ridge all night

effects.log: You sit on the widow Seo's ridge all night with your rice cake and watch the circles of fire on the dykes, and not one can leaves its string. In the morning the widow Seo comes out and bows to her own roof. It looks very strange from the lane.

choices.text: Show the children how to keep the coals from flying

effects.log: You sit on the edge of a can and glare at the coals until they settle. The child holding it learns, by watching, to swing smooth instead of hard. By the end of the night half the dyke is swinging smooth. The headman takes the credit. Of course.

events.text: A string snaps. A fire can goes over the dark like a comet and lands on the thatch of the widow Seo's house, and you are there before the thatch can take: you sit in the can on the hot coals as if it were a nest. And a child is coming up the persimmon tree after it, in socks, onto the roof. You know this. You have done this. Once you were the one climbing, and found a red bird sitting in your can.

choices.text: Hop out, and call every spark home

effects.log: You hop out of the can and call, and every spark in the thatch comes to you at once. The smoke stops. The child on the roof stares at you, mouth open, exactly as you once stared. Then you fly off into the dark, and leave the child to be got down with a ladder, because that is how it goes.

choices.text: Sit in the can and look at the child a while

effects.log: You sit on the coals and look at the child, and the child looks at you, and the thatch round the can goes out on its own because you will it to. It is a strange thing to be on the other side of a memory. You find you like it.

events.text: The can lands on the widow Seo's thatch and a child on the dyke starts shouting for water, loud enough to wake the whole valley. By the time the first bucket comes up the ladder there is nothing to put out: you have called the fire home and are sitting on the cold can on the ridge, preening. You remember shouting like that once, from the other side. And the boy from the next house, staring up at you now, says he is going to catch you.

choices.text: Preen, and let them all see you

effects.log: You preen on the ridge in front of the whole village with buckets in their hands. Half of them see you. The other half say the shouting child made it up. The boy from the next house says nothing more. He just looks, and remembers, and starts making plans.

choices.text: Fly off before anyone is sure

effects.log: You are gone over the paddies before the lamps come up. Nobody is sure of anything. Except the boy from the next house, who is very sure, and says so, at length, all spring.

events.text: The can lands on the widow Seo's thatch and begins to smoke, and down on the dyke one child does a strange thing: puts both hands together and bows, the way one bows at the new year, to whatever is moving on the roof. You know that bow from the inside. Once you made it, not knowing why. Now you are what it was made to.

choices.text: Lift the can off the thatch and set it on the ice

effects.log: You take the broken string in your beak and lift the can off the roof, quite easily, and carry it down to the frozen paddy and set it on the ice, and the thatch goes out behind you because it has nothing to burn. The child is still bowing when you fly off. You bow back, in the air, which is harder than it looks.

choices.text: Call the fire home, and bow back

effects.log: Every spark comes to you. Then you dip your head to the child on the dyke, once. The child does not tell anyone. Neither do you. There are some bows that only two people know about, and one of them is a bird.

events.text: The day before the first full moon, the young people of the village build the moon house on the riverbank: a cone of pine branches taller than three men, packed with straw, with a door facing the east where the moon will come up. Everybody ties a paper to it with a wish written on it. The children cannot write, so they draw. One drawing is of a red bird.

choices.text: Help them build it, carrying pine twigs

effects.log: You carry pine twigs to the top where nobody can reach and wedge them in, one by one, and by dusk the people building it are shouting up to you where the gaps are. It is the best-built moon house in years. Everybody says so. Nobody says how.

choices.text: Read the wishes, the ones that are written

effects.log: A good harvest. A son home from the coast. A cow that will not die. A husband who will stop. The ghost of a sister, to be at peace. Rain. Less rain. The moon house is full of what people cannot say aloud. You fly home very quiet.

events.text: Moonrise. The first edge of the moon comes up over the eastern hill, huge and gold, and the oldest man in the village puts the torch to the moon house, and it goes up all at once with a roar, and everyone shouts their wish at the same time, and the sparks go up and up toward the moon. You have never wanted anything more in your life than to be in that fire.

choices.text: Go in, and dance

effects.log: Into the heart of it, wings out, turning, and the fire turns with you, and from the riverbank the whole village sees a red bird dancing in the moon house with the moon behind it. Nobody shouts a wish for a while. Then everyone does, louder. It is going to be a lucky year. They are sure of it.

choices.text: Dance on the edge, where the wishes burn

effects.log: You go round and round the edge of the fire where the papers curl and blacken, and you carry each one up, gently, so it burns right through and the wish goes all the way to the moon. You do not know if it works. You do every one anyway.

choices.text: Watch from the willow, and keep it from the village

effects.log: You sit in the willow above the river and watch every spark, and when one drifts toward the thatch of the nearest house you go down and eat it. Somebody has to mind the fire while everybody else is happy. Tonight, you find, it is you.

events.text: Years after you danced in the moon house, the villagers are still talking about it. They build it bigger every year now, and leave a gap at the top shaped like a door for a bird. This year the headman's grandson, who is twelve, has climbed up into the gap to wait for you, which is a very bad idea, and is still up there when the old man lights the torch.

choices.text: Dive in and drive him out before the fire

ok.log: You come down on the boy like a hornet and peck and flap until he lets go, and he slides down the outside of the cone into the river shallows just as the straw catches. Wet, furious, alive. The headman beats him and then holds him for a long time.

fail.log: He will not let go, and the straw is already catching, and you have to hold the fire back from his side of the cone with everything you have until the men pull him down. He has a burnt sleeve. You have a burnt everything. (-8 health)

choices.text: Hold the fire back from his side until they get him down

effects.log: You sit in the fire and push it away from the boy with your whole body, the way you would push back a door against wind. The men pull him down. The moon house burns. Your feathers smell of pine for a month. (-6 health)

events.text: The third day of the third month, and they come back: two swallows, blue-black and quick, who go straight to the old mud nest under the kitchen eaves as if they had left it yesterday. They find a small bird asleep in it. "Excuse me," says one swallow. "That," says the other, "is our house."

choices.text: Move out, with apologies

effects.log: You climb out and sit on the beam beside it, and they move back in and start mending with mud at once, talking the whole time. By evening they have decided you can stay on the beam. It is warm there. They say the beam has never been so warm.

choices.text: Offer to keep their eggs warm

effects.log: They look at each other. A small bird that is warm and offers to sit on eggs. "Hm," says one. "Well," says the other. In the end you share. Swallows, it turns out, are very practical birds.

events.text: The swallows talk about the warm country as if it were the next village. Gangnam, they call it: south, over the sea, where it is never winter and the rice grows twice and the people are, well, all right. "Not as kind as here," says one. "We choose kind houses. We always choose kind houses. It is the rule."

choices.text: Ask how they know which houses are kind

effects.log: "You watch," says the swallow. "Who feeds the dog. Who shouts. Who leaves the eaves alone." Every eave in the country is watched by somebody who goes south and comes back and remembers. You find this both comforting and alarming.

choices.text: Ask the way south

effects.log: They tell you, place by place, the way you would tell the road to market: the river mouth, the islands, the strait, the long sea, a mountain like a sleeping ox. "You will not come," says one. "You are a stove bird." You are not sure that is true.

events.text: A storm in the night, and in the morning one of the swallows' fledglings is on the ground under the eaves with a leg folded the wrong way, and the parents are screaming overhead. The youngest of the house is already kneeling beside it in the mud with a strip of cotton thread and two slivers of bamboo, not sure, looking up at you.

choices.text: Hop down and keep the fledgling warm while it is bound

effects.log: You sit against the fledgling's side so it stops shaking, and the youngest binds the leg to the bamboo with red thread, very carefully, and you both put it back in the nest. The parents stop screaming. They look at you, after that, in a different way.

choices.text: Warm the bamboo and thread so they bend true

effects.log: You breathe on the slivers until they are supple and the thread until it is soft. The splint goes on clean and straight. The youngest gives you a look that says, I saw that. You give a look back that says, I know.

events.text: The third day of the third month again, and the swallows come back, and one of them, the young one, lands on the beam beside you and holds out its leg. There is still a thread of red cotton on it, faded pink. In its beak it has a seed, black and flat, the seed of a gourd.

choices.text: Take the seed and plant it by the fence

effects.log: It comes up by the fence in a week and climbs the thatch by midsummer, and in autumn there is one great white gourd on the roof. The house splits it at harvest. Inside: seeds, and good flesh, and nothing else at all. Not every story is that story. But the house eats well, and the swallow looks very pleased.

choices.text: Give the seed to the youngest, who mended the leg

effects.log: You drop it in the youngest's palm. The youngest plants it, waters it every evening, tells it stories. In autumn the gourd on the roof is the biggest in the village. When it is split it is full of nothing but seeds, and the youngest laughs and laughs and saves every one.

events.text: Autumn, and the swallows are gathering on the ridges of the village in long rows, chattering, getting ready for the road. The young one with the pink thread on its leg flies to you on the persimmon tree. "You are not a stove bird any more," it says. "You are red. Red birds go south. When you are ready, I will show you the road."

choices.text: Promise to go, one day

effects.log: "One day," you say. "When I am ready." The swallow looks at you sideways, the way swallows do. "Swallows do not wait," it says. "But I will, for you, a bit." They go at dawn, a black ribbon over the hill. You watch them till the sky is empty.

choices.text: Fly with them as far as the river mouth, and back

effects.log: You fly in the middle of the flock to the river mouth, where the land stops and the sea begins, grey and endless. The swallows go on over it without a pause. You turn back, your heart going like a kettle. Next time. Or the time after.

events.text: A sound in the rafters at dusk, a dry long sound, like a rope being drawn over wood. A rat snake, as long as the kitchen is wide, is coming along the beam toward the swallows' nest. The parents are out hunting. The nest is full of eggs. You are sitting beside it.

choices.text: Stand between the snake and the nest

effects.log: You plant yourself on the beam in front of the nest and fluff up every red feather you have. The snake stops, tongue flickering, considering a red sparrow. Snakes are patient. So, you are learning, are fires.

choices.text: Shriek for the parents

effects.log: You scream like a kettle, and the parents come in from the yard like two thrown knives, and the three of you dive at the snake together, and it stops halfway along the beam and thinks about it.

events.text: The snake does not go. It coils on the beam a body's length from the nest and lifts its head. It has eaten swallow eggs here before, you can tell; it knows the way. Your feathers are hot. Something in your breast is hotter. You have never in your life used fire to kill anything.

choices.text: Burn it off the beam

ok.log: You go at it with your whole heat, and the beam scorches in a bright streak, and the snake drops off into the woodpile with its skin smoking and goes, fast, and does not stop going. The first time fire was a weapon in you, and not only a warning. It was easy. That is what frightens you about it.

fail.log: It strikes before you are hot enough. Fangs in your shoulder; no poison, a rat snake, but it hurts like ice. You burn it off you and it drops away, scorched, and you sit on the beam and shake for an hour. (-14 health)
fail.deathCause: a rat snake in the rafters

choices.text: Heat the beam under it until it leaves

effects.log: You do not burn the snake. You burn the beam, slowly, until the wood under its belly is too hot to lie on. It shifts, and shifts, and gives up, and pours itself down the post and away. Nothing hurt but a beam and your own patience. (-3 health)

choices.text: Sit on the nest yourself, and dare it

effects.log: You climb in on top of the eggs and sit there, glowing, and stare at the snake. It stares back. It is still staring when the parents come home, and with three of you against it, it leaves. It does not come back to that beam. It goes to the next house, probably. You cannot sit on every nest.

events.text: Every swallow in the valley seems to know about the red bird and the snake. They come and look at you, two or three at a time, perched on the beam at a polite distance. Under the eaves of three different houses, they tell you, there is a snake in the rafters this spring. They would be grateful.

choices.text: Go to every house, and burn the beams under the snakes

effects.log: Three houses, three snakes, three scorched beams and nothing killed. The swallows of the valley start leaving you things: a shiny beetle, a bright thread, a flake of mica. You have been made something like an officer of the eaves. (-4 health)

choices.text: Tell them you are a fire, not a hawk

effects.log: "A fire is a guard," says the oldest swallow. "That is what fire is for, in a house." You think about that for a long time on your beam. You do not go. The next spring you do. (Smoulder +1)

events.text: A shadow goes over the paddies, fast and grey, and the sparrows on the fence are gone in one burst. A hawk, a young goshawk with jesses on its legs, a falconer's bird out for pheasant, and it has seen something red on the fence that is not a pheasant. It turns, high up, and comes down.

choices.text: Dive for the chimney

ok.log: Straight down the nearest chimney, wings tucked, and the hawk's talons close on smoke. You fall into a firebox in the dark and sit there gasping. When you come out at dusk you are black from beak to tail. Nobody recognises you for a week. It is extremely restful.

fail.log: A talon catches your back as you go down the chimney. You fall into the firebox, bleeding and black with soot, and lie there in the ash all night with your heart going like a drum. (-12 health)

choices.text: Turn and face it, red and hot

ok.log: You turn on the fence and flare, and the hawk, at the last instant, sees what it is stooping on and pulls up so hard it tumbles. It goes back to the falconer's glove with singed feet and a new opinion of sparrows.

fail.log: You flare, and the hawk does not care. It hits you like a thrown stone and you both go into the paddy, and you burn it until it lets go. You crawl out of the water under a hedge. You will not be on a fence again for a long time. (-16 health)
fail.deathCause: a falconer's hawk over the paddies

choices.text: Drop into the thick of the hedge

effects.log: Down into the thorns, deep, and the hawk cannot follow. It sits on the fence above you for an hour, looking. You sit in the thorns, looking back. Eventually the falconer whistles it in. (-3 health)

events.text: The falconer comes to the village to ask. He is a quiet hunter in a fur hat with the goshawk hooded on his fist, and he goes from house to house: has anyone seen a red bird? His hawk will not hunt. Since the day it stooped on the red thing on the fence, it sits on his glove and will not fly at anything. He has a family. The hawk is his living.

choices.text: Let the hawk see you again, and see you are only a bird

effects.log: You sit on the fence, red, quiet, small, and the falconer unhoods the hawk, and it looks at you a long time. You look back without flaring. Then it turns its head and looks at the hill, where the pheasants are. It flies. The falconer bows to the fence, puzzled, and goes home.

choices.text: Stay out of sight: a hawk that will not hunt is a good hawk

effects.log: You stay in the chimney. The falconer goes away with his hawk on his fist. You hear, later, that he sold it in the county town for a good price to a rich man who only wanted it to sit and look fine. Probably it is happy. Probably. (Smoulder +1)

events.text: Hawk weather: cold, clear, a high sky. You are on the ridge-pole of the great house when the shadow comes over again, and it is not the falconer's hawk this time but a wild one, older, with no jesses and no master, and it is not curious about red. It is hungry.

choices.text: Go down the chimney, where a hawk cannot follow

effects.log: Down the flue into the dark, and come out black with soot. It works. The children of the great house have a name for you now when you come out sooty: the crow that was a sparrow. (-2 health)

choices.text: Go up instead, higher than it, into the sun

ok.log: Up, up, into the glare, where a hawk cannot see a red bird against a white sun. You stay up until your wings shake and the hawk gives up and slides off down the valley. You come down knowing a thing: the sun is on your side.

fail.log: Up, but not fast enough. It catches you in the climb and you fall together, and you burn your way out of its grip and drop into a pine. (-10 health)

events.text: There is an old woman in the house across the lane, {npc}, who is older than anybody, and who greets {his} fire every morning. Not the kitchen god: the fire. "Good morning," {he} says, kneeling at the stove mouth. "Did you sleep? I did not. My hip." You have been sleeping in {his} stove this month, because it is the best-drawn stove in the lane, and you are not sure {he} has not noticed.
events.arc: The Grandmother Who Talks to the Fire

choices.text: Crackle back: good morning

effects.log: Snap, pop. {npc} stops. Then {he} laughs, a dry little laugh, and says, "There. I always said it was listening." {He} tells the fire about {his} hip, at length. You crackle in the right places.

choices.text: Stay quiet, and just burn well for {him}

effects.log: You keep {his} stove warm and even all morning and do not say a thing. {His} hip is better by noon. "You are a good fire," {he} says to it, as {he} says every day. Today it is true in a way {he} cannot know.

events.text: {npc} has decided you are a person. {He} sets a second bowl beside the bowl of water on the shelf, a little one, with a pinch of rice in it, and tells you the news: who is fighting, who is sick, which magistrate is a thief. "You will outlive me," {he} says one morning, quite cheerfully. "Fires do. Remember what I tell you."
events.arc: The Grandmother Who Talks to the Fire

choices.text: Remember everything {he} tells you

effects.log: Which wood smokes and which spits. How to bank a jar for three days. Why you never borrow fire, and why you always lend it. What a house sounds like before a quarrel. {He} has kept fires for seventy years. You will keep them for longer. You keep {his} first.

choices.text: Ask {him}, in pops and crackles, what a fire is for

effects.log: "For?" {He} laughs. "Rice. Warm feet. Light to sew by. Somebody to talk to." {He} pokes you, gently. "Kept fires are for keeping people. Wild ones are for nothing. Remember that." You do.
