events.text: {npc}'s family do not believe {him}. {His} son's wife says to the neighbours that the old one talks to the stove, poor thing, and the grandson laughs out loud at the little bowl of rice. This morning, in front of all of them, {npc} kneels and says to the stove, "Show them. Go on. Just once."
events.arc: The Grandmother Who Talks to the Fire

choices.text: Show them: rise up out of the firebox, red

effects.log: You come up out of the stove mouth like a sunrise, a red bird, and sit on the lip and look at the son's wife. The son's wife sits down on the floor. The grandson drops the spoon. {npc} does not even look round. "There," {he} says, very satisfied. Nobody laughs at the little bowl of rice again.

choices.text: Flare the fire up so high the rice boils over at once

effects.log: Whoosh. The pot boils over in a cloud of steam. Nobody sees a bird, but everyone sees a fire do what it was asked to. The grandson stops laughing. The son's wife says it was a draught. {npc} says nothing, and pats the stove.

choices.text: Do nothing: it is not a thing to show

effects.log: You stay low. {npc} waits, and waits, and gets up stiffly, and the grandson laughs. That night {npc} sits by the stove and does not talk to you. The next morning {he} does again. You do not know if you were right. (Smoulder +1)

events.text: {npc} does not kneel at the stove this morning. {He} is lying on the warm floor of the inner room with the quilt up to {his} chin, and the family are sitting round {him}, and the stove is unlit because nobody has thought of it. {He} turns {his} head a little toward the kitchen door. "Who is keeping my fire?" {he} says.
events.arc: The Grandmother Who Talks to the Fire

choices.text: Light the stove yourself, and keep the floor warm under {him}

effects.npcPass: old age, on a warm floor
effects.log: You go into the cold stove and burn, and the floor under {him} warms, slowly, all through the long morning. "Ah," {he} says. "There it is." {He} dies at noon, warm. You keep that stove lit for the forty-nine days, and nobody in the family ever lets it go out again.

choices.text: Come in and sit on the quilt by {his} hand

effects.npcPass: old age, with a red bird on the quilt
effects.log: You come in through the paper door, in front of everyone, and sit on the quilt beside {his} hand. {He} moves {his} fingers into your feathers. "Warm," {he} says. "I told them." {He} goes to sleep and does not wake. The family say nothing at all about the bird, then or ever.

events.text: A boy from the next house, {npc}, about ten, with a sling in {his} belt and burrs on {his} trousers, has decided you are the most interesting thing in the village. {He} follows you. {He} throws pebbles near you, not at you, quite. This morning {he} creeps up behind you on the wall while you are sunning, and {his} hand closes on your tail.

choices.text: Hold still and let {him} look

effects.log: You hold still. {npc} holds your tail and stares at you, and you stare back over your shoulder. "You are hot," {he} says, amazed. {He} lets go before it can burn {him}, a long red tail feather left behind in {his} fist, and stares at it as if it were gold. Not a bad child. Only a child.

choices.text: Pull free and fly

effects.log: You yank, and fly, and leave one long red tail feather in {his} fist. {He} stands in the lane looking at it as if it were gold. It is the first piece of you anyone has kept on purpose.

events.text: {npc} again, with friends this time, three children on the wall, and {he} is showing off. "Watch," {he} says, "I can catch it," and {he} grabs, and gets your tail properly, and pulls, and it hurts, and the others laugh, and something in you that has never been angry before goes white.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You take the white heat and swallow it, down, into your crop, where it sits like a hot stone. Your eyes water. {npc} lets go, a little frightened by the look of you, and the others go off laughing. The stone stays. You will have to do something with it one day. (Smoulder +3, -2 health)

choices.text: Peck {his} hand, hard, and nothing more

ok.log: A sharp peck, a yelp, and {he} lets go. No fire. Just a small red bird that will not be grabbed. The others laugh at {npc} instead. It is, you think, exactly enough.

fail.log: You peck, and the heat comes out with the peck, and {his} sleeve smokes, and {his} sandals catch, and {he} is hopping in the lane before you know what you did. A peck is never only a peck, for you. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: Heat, all at once, out of you like a breath. {npc}'s straw sandals catch. {He} hops and shrieks and kicks them off into the ditch, and they burn there, and the others run. Nobody is really hurt. A pair of sandals is gone that a poor house could not spare. The first thing you ever burned in anger. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Swallow it, and fail

effects.log: You try to swallow it. There is no room left in you. It goes down and comes straight back up as fire, and {npc}'s sandals burn anyway, and you have the hot stone too. (Smoulder +3, Ash +1, -2 health)

events.text: {npc}'s family are at the well, telling everyone there that the red bird is a demon, that it burned their child, that someone should get the shaman, or a net, or both. {npc} is standing behind them, quiet, with {his} hands behind {his} back. In one of them, you can see from the wall, is your first tail feather.

choices.text: Land on the well rim in front of all of them

effects.log: You land on the well rim, red and calm, and look at them all. The talk stops. The others at the well look at you, and at the family, and at {npc}. Somebody laughs. "A demon, that size?" The talk at the well goes on to other things. {npc} watches you all the way home.

choices.text: Leave a new pair of straw sandals at their gate

effects.log: It takes you three nights to steal the straw and a week of being laughed at by sparrows to plait it, beak and claw. They are terrible sandals. They are on the gate in the morning. {npc}'s family stare at them a long time, then put them on {npc}'s feet without a word.

choices.text: Stay away from that lane for a year

effects.log: You go round. The talk dies down, as talk does. In the autumn {npc} is seen, the neighbours say, sitting on the wall where you used to sun yourself, waiting, with the red feather stuck in {his} topknot.

events.text: {npc} is grown now, with a farmer's hands and a family and a crooked nose from a fight in the market, and {he} still wears the red feather, faded orange, in {his} headband. {He} sees you on the wall where it all began. {He} does not grab. {He} sits down at the other end of the wall, slowly, the way you sit near a skittish horse.

choices.text: Sit with {him} a while

effects.log: "I was a horrible child," {he} says to the paddies. You agree, in your way. {He} laughs. You sit together on the wall until the light goes. It is not forgiveness exactly. It is something that does just as well.

choices.text: Hop along the wall, closer, and let {him} see you up close

effects.log: Hop by hop, until you are a hand's length from {him}. {He} does not move. {He} looks at you the way {he} looked at the feather at ten. "You are still hot," {he} says. "Good." {His} children, later, are the only ones in the village who never throw stones at birds.

events.text: The boy from the next house has a plan. You can tell. He has a basket propped on a stick with a string tied to it and a heap of grain under it, and he lies behind the woodpile every afternoon holding the string. Since the night of the fire can on the roof, he has told everyone he will catch the red bird. It is a very old trap. You remember it from the other side: once you watched someone swear this oath with a bucket in your hands.

choices.text: Walk in under the basket and out again, slowly

effects.log: You walk under the basket, eat one grain, and walk out. The basket comes down a breath too late. You do it again. And again. By the fourth time he is laughing too hard to pull the string.

choices.text: Let him catch you, once

effects.log: Down comes the basket and you sit under it, glowing, and the wicker starts to smoke. He lifts it in a hurry. You walk out past his nose, and he lets you, and he never sets the trap again. Some oaths are kept by being let go of.

events.text: Someone says it again. At the well, on the wall, in the lane: "a scorched sparrow", "the kitchen's chicken", "the bird that eats ash". Somebody's child throws a clod of earth after you and somebody's grandfather laughs. It is a small thing. Everything in you that is fire says it is not.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You swallow it. Down into the crop, onto whatever is already there. It is getting to be quite a pile. (Smoulder +3, -2 health)

choices.text: Laugh it off, and fly away high

effects.log: You laugh, a chirping, crackling laugh, and go up so high the words cannot follow. Up there it is only wind. It works, this time. Laughter is a fire too, you are beginning to suspect, and a dangerous one.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: A flare, and the clod of earth bursts into dust in the air, and the grandfather's straw hat smoulders at the brim. He beats it out. Nobody laughs any more. Nobody thanks you either. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Swallow it, and fail

effects.log: You try to swallow it and it will not go down; there is too much down there already. It comes out by itself, a flare that singes the grandfather's hat and the child's sleeve, and you still feel the stone. (Smoulder +3, Ash +1, -2 health)

events.text: Up the valley, in the oak woods, there is smoke that never flames. You follow it to a clearing where three charcoal burners have built a dome of clay over a stack of oak logs as high as a house, lit it, and sealed it. It breathes a thin blue smoke through little holes. It will burn like that, they say, for a week. Without a flame. You do not understand at all how a fire can do that.

choices.text: Sit on the dome and feel it

effects.log: The clay under you is as hot as a stove lid, and inside, under it, a whole house of oak is burning with no air and no light, slowly, patiently, turning into something harder than itself. You sit there all night and feel it think.

choices.text: Ask the burners, in your way, how it is done

effects.log: The youngest burner, a lanky one who talks to everything, explains it to the bird on the woodpile as if you were a new hand: the stack, the clay, the vents, the colour of the smoke, when to close a hole. "Patience," the burner says. "Fire wants to be fast. You make it wait." You stare.

events.text: The fourth day of the burn. The smoke from one vent has gone the wrong colour, yellow and thick, and the burners are arguing: open it and the whole kiln may catch and burn to ash; leave it and the stack may go out. They have a week's oak and a winter's living in that dome.

choices.text: Go in through the vent and settle the fire

ok.log: In through the hole into the heavy dark, and you find the place where the fire has woken up too much, and you sit on it and hold it down, slow, slow, the way you hold yourself small in a cold jar. The smoke goes blue again. The burners never know why. You come out a day later than you went in, very calm.

fail.log: In through the hole, and the heat inside is not like any heat you know: thick, airless, patient as stone. You barely get out. The burners open the vent anyway and the kiln is saved by luck. You lie in the snow for an hour, steaming. (-8 health)

choices.text: Watch, and learn what they do

effects.log: The oldest burner closes the vent with a handful of wet clay, and opens another on the far side, and waits. Half a day. The smoke turns blue. Nobody shouts. You learn that most of keeping a fire is waiting to see what it does next.

events.text: Midnight, the seventh day, and the burners break the seal. They draw the charcoal out with long iron hooks, white hot, ringing like bells when it knocks together, and throw sand and ash over it to cool. In the morning it is black and light and hard, and it will burn hotter and cleaner than the oak ever could. The lanky burner holds up a piece. "There," the burner says to you. "That is what waiting makes."

choices.text: Take a piece of charcoal to keep

effects.log: A small piece, rung like a bell. You carry it to the widow's fence, or the kitchen shelf, or wherever you sleep that year. Whenever you are about to flare, you look at it. It helps. Not always.

choices.text: Sit in the cooling kiln all morning

effects.log: The empty dome is the warmest place in the world, a slow, even, patient heat that goes right into the bone. You sleep there all morning and dream of nothing at all. The burners leave you a rice ball on the threshold.

events.text: No rain since the barley harvest. The paddies are grey and cracked like an old bowl, the stream is stones, and the heat comes down off the hills every noon like a lid. And you, you find, are hot. Every feather. Every breath. Wherever you sit, the straw under you crackles. You have never been a fire in a dry year before.

choices.text: Sleep in the well-house, in the cool

effects.log: Down into the stone well-house where the air is damp and the water is still cold at the bottom, and you sleep on the wet stones all through the heat of every day. You come out only at dusk. You learn that a fire can choose when to be a fire.

choices.text: Keep flying, high, away from the dry straw

effects.log: Up where the air is thin and cool, hour after hour, until your wings ache. Nothing below catches from you. It is very lonely up there, keeping your heat away from everything that could burn.

choices.text: Sit on the thatch as you always do

effects.log: You sit on the great house's ridge as you always have, and by afternoon a ring of thatch round you is smouldering, and a servant on a ladder is throwing water at you. You were not angry. You were only there. That, you learn, is enough, in a dry year. (Ash +1)

events.text: The village holds a rain rite on the hill, the headman in his best robe and a pig's head on the altar and a shaman with a fan, and you come to watch. The shaman spins, and stops, and points straight at you on the pine branch. "There," she cries. "The red one. That is the heat. That is why it does not rain." Every face turns.

choices.text: Fly off, far, until the rains come

effects.log: You go. Over the hills, a long way, to a valley that had its rain. It is not your doing, the drought; you know it is not. But you are part of the heat, and the heat has to go somewhere. It rains in your village nine days later. You hear it from a swallow.

choices.text: Stay on the branch and let them look

effects.log: You stay. Somebody throws a stone. Then another. You sit through it and swallow it, every stone, until the shaman herself tells them to stop, frightened by how still you are. It rains a week later, and nobody apologises. (Smoulder +2)

choices.text: Bow to the altar, as they do

effects.log: You hop down onto the altar beside the pig's head and bow to the sky, as they are bowing. The shaman stares. The headman, after a moment, bows beside you. It rains that night, by chance or not, and the village is not sure, after that, what you are.

events.text: The rain comes at last, warm and heavy, straight down, and the whole village runs out into it with their faces up. The cracks in the paddies close like mouths. You sit under the eaves, very dry, very small, steaming at the edges, and watch it, and for the first time in your life you are a little afraid of a thing that is not a hawk or a cat.

choices.text: Go out into it

effects.log: You go out and stand in it. It hisses on you. It hurts, like cold water on a hot pan, and you stand there anyway until the hissing stops, and then you are only a wet red bird in the rain, and it is not so bad. (-4 health)

choices.text: Stay under the eaves and watch the paddies drink

effects.log: You watch until dark. Fire and water, you think. Every summer the one, every autumn the other. Somewhere east of here, the swallows say, there is a blue dragon that does nothing but bring rain. You hope you never have to argue with it.

events.text: The smithy at the crossroads: a stone forge like a little oven, a push-pull bellows, an anvil worn into a dip, and the smith, {npc}, a broad quiet person with burn scars up both arms, making sickles for the harvest. The bellows go whump, whump, and the coals go white, and you are sitting on the rafter above the forge with your eyes half shut, because it is the most beautiful sound you have ever heard.

choices.text: Drop down into the forge

effects.log: Into the white coals, which are like a warm bath. {npc} stops the bellows and stares at the red bird in the forge. Then, slowly, {he} puts the sickle blank in beside you, and starts the bellows again. Neither of you says anything. It is the start of a friendship.

choices.text: Watch the bellows, and learn the breath

effects.log: In, out, in, out: the bellows breathe for the fire, and the fire grows. You breathe with them all afternoon, and by evening you can make yourself burn white for three whole breaths. {npc} notices the bird on the rafter breathing in time, and laughs for the first time that day.

events.text: {npc} has noticed that the iron is better on the days the red bird sits in the forge. Harder. Truer. The sickles take an edge and keep it all harvest. {He} says nothing about it to anyone, but the neighbours notice the sickles, and so do the villages over the hill, and there is a line at the smithy door that was never there before.

choices.text: Sit in the forge for every sickle and hoe

effects.log: All autumn you sit in the forge, and the valley cuts its rice with the best sickles in the province. {npc} saves the scraps of rice from {his} lunch for you on the anvil. You do not eat rice. You eat it anyway.

choices.text: Only on the days {he} asks

effects.log: {npc} learns to ask: a look up at the rafter, a nod at the coals. You come down when asked and not otherwise. A fire that comes when it is called and not when it is not: you suspect this is a thing you will need to be good at.

events.text: A rider at the smithy, in a fine coat with a sword at the hip, from some school of the martial roads, who has heard about the sickles and wants a blade. Not a sickle. A sword, forged in the bird's fire. A purse goes down on the anvil. {npc} looks at the purse, and then up at the rafter, at you.

choices.text: Fly off the rafter and out of the door

effects.log: You go out through the smoke-hole. {npc} pushes the purse back across the anvil. "The bird does not do swords," {he} says, as if {he} had always known it. The rider goes away angry. You do not know yet why you went. Someday you will.

choices.text: Stay, and let {him} decide

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. Then {he} takes the purse and makes a sword. You sit in the forge for it, because you said you would let {him} decide. It is a very good sword. You do not like knowing it is out there. (Smoulder +1)

choices.text: Flare white and scorch the purse

effects.log: The purse on the anvil goes up in a puff of silk and the coins drop through it, blackened. The rider stares at the bird on the rafter, at the smith, at the blackened money. The coins stay where they fell. The rider leaves, quickly. (Ash +1)

events.text: You wake one morning in the fire jar and something is wrong with your wing. You turn your head to look. One feather, at the tip, is not grey. It is red, the red of the inside of a coal, so red it seems to glow in the dark of the jar. By the end of the month there are nine.

choices.text: Show it to everyone

effects.log: You sit on the stove, the jar, the gatepost, the ridge, holding your wing out. "It is red," says the kitchen god, unimpressed. "We noticed." The children notice. The sparrows notice. Grey to red: you are a different bird, and the whole lane can see it.

choices.text: Preen it, alone, for a long time

effects.log: You sit in the jar and look at it. It is you. It was always you, under the grey. You preen it into place, very carefully, and do not show anyone for a week, and the week is the happiest of your life.

events.text: The grey goes all at once in the spring moult, the soft ash-coloured down coming out of you in tufts all over the kitchen floor. {npc} gathers it up with the hearth brush, and then stops, and picks one grey feather out of the ash, and holds it up to the light, and does not throw it away.

choices.text: Let {him} keep it

effects.log: {npc} folds it into a twist of paper and keeps it in {his} sewing box for the rest of {his} life. When {he} is old {he} shows it to grandchildren: the first feather of the red bird, from when it was grey. They do not believe {him}. The feather, if you hold it, is warm.

choices.text: Give {him} a red one too

effects.log: You pull one of the new red ones and drop it in {his} hand beside the grey. It hurts. {He} holds the two of them side by side, grey and red, and looks at you for a long time. "Before and after," {he} says. "I knew you before." (-2 health)
